card werk-stack-framework  [decided]
Client framework: React + Vite
why: Eryk decided. Criterion 2 (state-preserving per-component HMR) and criterion 6 (agent proficiency) both point at React, and neither runner-up wins them back.

React + Vite. Vite runs as the CLIENT dev server, in middleware mode, inside werk's own Bun server. It is not the server runtime — that is why this does not contradict #werk-hmr, which rejected **vite-node as the process host** after it crashed werk outright (#werk-hmr:src2). One process: Bun serves the API and the SSE stream and hot-reloads its own modules. Vite transforms and hot-reloads the client.

## Why, against the six criteria

1. **Component architecture** — React. Every candidate satisfied this.
2. **Per-component HMR preserving state** — the discriminator. React Fast Refresh preserves hook state per component. It is the most proven implementation of this requirement. Every rejected option lost or weakened it: Lit has no equivalent (#werk-stack:opt0), Solid remounts (#werk-stack:opt2), svelte-hmr is less reliable for the case that matters (#werk-stack:opt3). werk's chat pane holds a live SSE stream and an in-flight turn. A remount on save is the failure this criterion exists to prevent.
6. **Agent proficiency** — React by a wide margin. Eryk ranked this alongside criterion 2. It is why the Svelte 5 runner-up lost: runes are recent enough that agents still reach for Svelte 4 store idioms.

Criteria 3, 4, and 5 do not discriminate between frameworks — see #werk-stack-hydration and #werk-hmr.

The three rejected options are #werk-stack:opt0, #werk-stack:opt2, #werk-stack:opt3, each with its own why_not.

  -> depends_on      werk-hmr  Rebuild werk's dev server on a stack with HMR that survives its own edits
  <- alternative_to  werk-stack:opt0  Stay vanilla. Add web components or Lit for structure
  <- alternative_to  werk-stack:opt2  SolidJS with Vite

card werk-hmr  [decided]
Rebuild werk's dev server on a stack with HMR that survives its own edits
why: Settled by research, two rounds of real-app testing, a direct repro of the one open correctness concern, and Eryk's own priorities on productionization and upgrade risk. See #werk-hmr:src0 through src5, and options opt1/opt2.

The agent's job includes editing werk's own source. A restart-based reload cannot support that: it kills the live claude child mid-turn every time the agent saves a file it is working through. Needs a stack where a code edit reloads the changed module without killing the process holding open child sessions.

Research (#werk-hmr:src0): vite-node invalidates transitively, not globally. Bun --hot guarantees globalThis survives. Deno --watch-hmr names an in-flight async function as a forced-full-restart case, the exact shape of werk's failure. Node core has no HMR.

Toy prototype (#werk-hmr:src1): a minimal Agent-shaped harness, globalThis-pinned, survived edits to both a sibling module and the pinned module itself, under both bun --hot and vite-node --watch.

Real-app test, unpatched (#werk-hmr:src2): werk's real code has neither guard. vite-node --watch crashed outright on an unrelated-file edit (EADDRINUSE retry loop, process.exit(1)). bun --hot did not crash, but silently orphaned a live task on the same edit.

Fix, real-app test, patched (#werk-hmr:src3): one guard clause in server.ts's serve() (globalThis.__werkServe check) fixed both candidates identically. Both now survive a real in-flight task through a src edit, verified with a fresh-connection check. Side effect worth knowing: this guard also means a hot reload stops applying code changes inside serve()'s body - the tradeoff is 'my live session survives an edit' over 'my latest route-handler edit is live', which is correct for the original problem.

# werk — instructions for the agent

This repository builds its own design tool. Use the tool while you build it.

## Keep the map current, every turn

When the conversation settles something, append it to the log **in the same turn**:

```bash
node src/cli.ts add <id> --title "..." --why "..." --parent <id> --status <s> --who <w>
node src/cli.ts link <from> <to> --type depends_on
node src/cli.ts status <id> decided
node src/cli.ts reopen <id>
```

Do not batch this up for later. The map is the record of what the conversation established.
The transcript is not.

## After a structural map change, ask whether the diagram should move too

`.werk/diagram-grid-full-minimal.wgrid` is a second, hand-authored description of the product
— see #vi-sysdiag-grain and #vi-sysdiag-derive. It does not update itself, and nothing in the
log keeps it in sync.

Only a **decided** card may justify diagram content. At the end of any turn where you added,
retitled, relinked, or changed the decided-status of a card that names a real running part of
the system — not a note, not a why-only edit — spawn two subagents in order, in the same turn.
A status change is exactly the trigger, not an exception to it: a card becoming decided can
add content, and a decided card being reopened removes its standing to justify any — see
#vi-sysdiag-agents.

1. `sysdiag-scout` — tell it exactly what changed: the ids, the operations, the before/after
   titles or edges. It reads the current diagram and reports whether it still matches, and if
   not, the precise content-section change needed.
2. If it reports a change, `sysdiag-updater` — hand it that report verbatim. It edits the
   `.wgrid` file and rebuilds with `bun src/gridsys/build.ts` until the tile grammar (R1–R6,
   see `src/gridsys/check.ts`) passes with 0 errors.

Most turns end at step 1 with `NO CHANGE NEEDED`: most decided cards are about the map itself,
not about a drawable part of the product. Do not force a diagram edit to justify running these.

## Eryk refers to cards by id

An id looks like `#werk-excerpt`. When he pastes `re #<id> "<title>": ...`, he typed that in
the map. Run `node src/cli.ts inbox` to read the whole thread, then reply with
`node src/cli.ts say <id> "..."` so the answer lands on the card, not only in the terminal.

## Record `depends_on` at the moment you create a card

A single-hop model check recovers only 6% to 11% of an invalidation chain. There is no way
to reconstruct these edges later. If a card is true only because another card is true, write
the edge now, or staleness propagation is dead and the map rots into a pretty outline.

`refines` is where a card **sits**. `depends_on` is what a card **needs**. They are different
graphs over the same nodes. That is the whole point.

## Record a rejected option the moment you weigh it

When a decision comes from real contrast in conversation — you named an alternative, gave a
reason, and rejected it — add that alternative as its own `option` node with `--why_not`, and
link it `alternative_to` the decided card, in the same turn:

```bash
node src/cli.ts add <id>:opt0 --kind option --title "..." --why_not "..."
node src/cli.ts link <id>:opt0 <id> --type alternative_to
```

If you skip this, the card is indistinguishable later from one decided with no contrast at
all — the `unchallenged` marker cannot tell "no option was weighed" from "an option was
weighed but never written down." Both #ro-unchal and #vi-backend were corrected after the
fact because of this. Do not create a third case.

## Say so when a card you just made comes out stale

A new card inherits a reopen from anywhere upstream of its `depends_on` targets, however many
hops away. It turns red the moment you create it, and Eryk sees the red mark before he sees
your message. Say it yourself in the same turn: name the origin, and say the card was written
with that correction already in hand.

A rule for any module in any project on this platform, not only werk's four files today.

**1. Classify the module by one question.** Does a wrong line throw, hang, or crash — or does it quietly produce a result that looks correct? A quiet wrong answer is pure. A loud failure is I/O.

**2. Pure code gets a number.** A pure module is a plain function of its input, cheap to call from a test, and a bug in it never announces itself. Set a high line-coverage threshold. Testing it is cheap and missing a bug in it is expensive, so a hard number belongs here.

**3. I/O code gets a named list, never a percentage.** An I/O module holds something live — a child process, a socket, an open file, a network call. Covering a line here means faking the live thing, and a percentage rewards the fake, not the real risk. Write one list per module instead: named behaviours, no number.

**4. Find the behaviours by sampling, not by guessing.** Run several independent readings of the module against one brief: name what breaks the tool if this is wrong. Where the readings agree, that is the list. Where they disagree, the disagreement is a fact question about the code, not a taste question — read the source and settle it. Do not ask a person to guess at what code already does.

**5. Write each behaviour as a responsibility, not as a location.** 'A crash never loses the in-flight message' survives a rewrite. 'agent.ts line 326 throws' does not. A list built this way stays true when the file under it changes, as long as the module's job stays the same. Only a changed responsibility needs the list re-run — not a renamed file or a moved line.
